content: Oregano, also known as Pot Marjoram (scientific name: Origanum vulgare), is a perennial herb that originates from Europe, the Mediterranean region, and parts of southern and central Asia. The plant produces purple flowers that are 3-4 mm long and arranged in upright spikes. The name oregano is derived from the Greek word origanon, which combines oros (meaning mountain) and the verb ganousthai (meaning to delight in). Cultivation and Culinary Uses The subspecies Origanum vulgare hirtum is a significant culinary herb, particularly prominent in Greek and Italian cuisines. The leaves of the plant are used in cooking, and the dried form of oregano is often more potent in flavor than the fresh leaves. Oregano is a common ingredient in tomato-based sauces, fried vegetables, and grilled meats. Alongside basil, it plays a key role in defining the characteristic flavor of many Italian dishes. It pairs well with pickled olives, capers, and lovage leaves. Unlike most Italian herbs, oregano complements hot and spicy dishes, which are popular in southern Italy. In Greek cuisine, oregano is indispensable. It enhances the flavor of Greek salads and is frequently used either on its own or as part of a lemon-olive oil sauce that accompanies grilled fish, meat, and certain casseroles. Oregano has an aromatic, warm, and slightly bitter taste, with its intensity varying depending on the quality. High-quality oregano can be so strong that it almost numbs the tongue, whereas cultivars grown in colder climates often have a less satisfactory flavor. The composition of oregano's essential oil is influenced more by factors such as climate, season, and soil than by differences between species. Other species closely related to oregano include Origanum onites (native to Greece and Asia Minor) and Origanum heracleoticum (found in Italy, the Balkan Peninsula, and West Asia), both of which have similar flavors. Marjoram, a related plant from Asia Minor, differs significantly in taste due to the absence of phenolic compounds in its essential oil. Some hybrid varieties exhibit a flavor profile that is intermediate between oregano and marjoram. Oregano is most famously associated with pizza, and its relatives have likely been consumed in southern Italy for centuries. Health Benefits Oregano is rich in antioxidants, primarily due to its high content of phenolic acids and flavonoids. These compounds contribute to its ability to neutralize free radicals (as supported by studies with PMID 16218659 and PMID 12730411). Additionally, oregano has demonstrated antimicrobial properties, particularly against foodborne pathogens such as Listeria monocytogenes (PMID 16218659). These attributes make oregano potentially beneficial for both health and food preservation. In the Philippines, oregano (Coleus aromaticus) is not commonly used in cooking but is instead valued as a medicinal plant, particularly for alleviating coughs in children. Other Plants Referred to as Oregano Mexican oregano (Lippia graveolens), which belongs to the Verbenaceae family, is closely related to lemon verbena. This herb has been extensively studied for its medicinal properties and is commonly used in traditional curandera (female shamanic) practices in Mexico and the Southwestern United States. Mexican oregano has a flavor profile similar to that of traditional oregano but is generally stronger. It is becoming increasingly available outside of Mexico, particularly in the United States. It is sometimes used as a substitute for epazote leaves, although the reverse substitution is not effective. Several other plants are also referred to as oregano in different regions of Mexico. These include Poliomintha longiflora, Lippia berlandieri, and Plectranthus amboinicus (synonym: Coleus aromaticus), which is also known as Cuban oregano.
